title: Atoms, Trends & Bonding
description: Electron configurations and their exceptions, periodic trends with reasons, lattice energy, formal charge, VSEPR, hybridization, polarity and IMFs.

cards.title: Avogadro's number: how many particles are in one mole of a substance? (4 significant figures)
cards.body:
$6.022\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$

The **mole** is defined by fixing $N_A$ at exactly $6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$ (2019 SI redefinition). A mole of $^{12}\ce{C}$ atoms has a mass of about $12\,\mathrm{g}$, and each atom has a mass of $12\,\mathrm{u}$.

Example: $0.50\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\ce{CO2}$ is $3.0\times10^{23}$ molecules but $9.0\times10^{23}$ atoms.
Watch out: to count atoms, multiply by the number of atoms per formula unit (3 here).
cards.searchQuery: Avogadro number value mole particles

cards.title: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in the ion $^{37}\ce{Cl^-}$ ($Z = 17$)?
cards.body:
17 protons, 20 neutrons, 18 electrons.

Neutrons $= A - Z = 37 - 17 = 20$. The $1-$ charge means one **extra electron** beyond the 17 protons.

$^{35}\ce{Cl}$ and $^{37}\ce{Cl}$ are isotopes: same $Z$, different neutron counts, essentially the same chemistry.
Tip: protons $= Z$; electrons $= Z -$ charge; neutrons $= A - Z$.
cards.searchQuery: protons neutrons electrons chloride ion Cl-37

cards.title: How many orbitals are in the $n = 3$ shell?
cards.body:
9 orbitals ($n^2$).

$\ell$ runs from 0 to $n-1$ (3s, 3p, 3d) and $m_\ell$ from $-\ell$ to $+\ell$, giving $1 + 3 + 5 = 9$ orbitals. They hold $2n^2 = 18$ electrons.

Watch out: $n = 2$ with $\ell = 2$ is not allowed, because $\ell \le n - 1$.
cards.searchQuery: number of orbitals in n=3 shell n squared

cards.title: Which rule says nitrogen's three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins instead of pairing up?
cards.body:
Hund's rule.

Electrons enter **degenerate orbitals** singly, with parallel spins, before any pairing. This minimizes electron-electron repulsion.

Its partners: Aufbau (fill the lowest-energy orbitals first) and Pauli (at most 2 electrons per orbital, with opposite spins).
Example: nitrogen's 2p electrons are $\uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow$, not $\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\ \_$.
cards.searchQuery: Hund's rule electron configuration nitrogen 2p

cards.title: What are the actual ground-state electron configurations of chromium ($\ce{Cr}$) and copper ($\ce{Cu}$)?
cards.body:
$\ce{Cr}$: $\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^5\,4s^1}$ and $\ce{Cu}$: $\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10}\,4s^1}$

Not the "expected" $\mathrm{3d^4\,4s^2}$ and $\mathrm{3d^9\,4s^2}$. A **half-filled or completely filled d subshell** is especially stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d.

Key idea: $\ce{Mo}$ and $\ce{Ag}$ follow the same pattern in the next period.
cards.searchQuery: chromium copper electron configuration exception

cards.title: Why does atomic radius decrease from left to right across a period but increase down a group?
cards.body:
Across: $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ rises, pulling the same valence shell closer. Down: each period adds a shell with higher $n$, farther from the nucleus.

Protons are added across a period, but same-shell electrons shield each other poorly, so **effective nuclear charge** climbs.

Example: $\ce{Na} > \ce{Mg} > \ce{Cl}$ and $\ce{Li} < \ce{Na} < \ce{K}$.
cards.searchQuery: atomic radius periodic trend effective nuclear charge

cards.title: First ionization energy generally rises across period 2. Why is it lower for $\ce{O}$ than for $\ce{N}$, and for $\ce{B}$ than for $\ce{Be}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{O}$: its fourth 2p electron is paired, and the extra electron-electron repulsion makes it easier to remove. $\ce{B}$: its outer electron is in 2p, higher in energy than 2s and partly shielded by the 2s electrons.

$\ce{N}$'s half-filled $\mathrm{2p^3}$ has no paired electrons, so it holds on tightly.

Key idea: $IE_1$ generally rises across a period ($Z_\mathrm{eff}$ up) and falls down a group (larger atoms).
Watch out: the dips are at group 13 (below group 2) and group 16 (below group 15).
cards.searchQuery: first ionization energy exceptions oxygen nitrogen boron beryllium

cards.title: An element has $IE_1 = 738$, $IE_2 = 1451$ and $IE_3 = 7733\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. Which group of the periodic table is it in?
cards.body:
Group 2 (alkaline earth metals); the element is $\ce{Mg}$.

The huge jump after $IE_2$ means the third electron must come from the **noble-gas core**. The number of electrons removed before the big jump equals the number of valence electrons.

Tip: look for the first jump of roughly 4 to 10 times the previous value.
cards.searchQuery: successive ionization energies large jump group

cards.title: Arrange $\ce{Si}$, $\ce{C}$, $\ce{N}$, $\ce{O}$ and $\ce{F}$ in order of increasing electronegativity.
cards.body:
$\ce{Si} < \ce{C} < \ce{N} < \ce{O} < \ce{F}$

Electronegativity rises across a period and up a group ($\ce{Si}$ sits below $\ce{C}$). Higher $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ and a smaller radius let the nucleus pull bonding electrons harder.

Key idea: $\ce{F}$ (about 4.0 on the Pauling scale) is the most electronegative element.
cards.searchQuery: electronegativity trend order Si C N O F

cards.title: Which has the largest lattice energy (in magnitude): $\ce{KCl}$, $\ce{NaCl}$, $\ce{NaF}$ or $\ce{MgO}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{MgO}$

Lattice energy is roughly $3800\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ for $\ce{MgO}$, versus about $790\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ for $\ce{NaCl}$.

Why: Coulomb's law gives lattice energy $\propto q_1q_2/r$. $\ce{Mg^2+}$ and $\ce{O^2-}$ have 4 times the charge product of a $1+/1-$ pair, and both ions are small.
Tip: among $1+/1-$ salts, smaller ions win: $\ce{NaF} > \ce{NaCl} > \ce{KCl}$.
cards.searchQuery: lattice energy MgO NaCl comparison charge size

cards.title: In the best Lewis structure of carbon monoxide, $\ce{:C≡O:}$, what is the formal charge on carbon?
cards.body:
$-1$

Formula: $FC = V - N - B/2$, using valence ($V$), nonbonding ($N$) and bonding ($B$) electrons. For carbon: $4 - 2 - 6/2 = -1$; oxygen is $+1$.

The triple bond gives both atoms an **octet**, which matters more than putting the negative charge on the more electronegative atom.
Watch out: CO is a rare case where the formal charges go "the wrong way" and the structure is still best.
cards.searchQuery: formal charge carbon monoxide carbon -1

cards.title: What is the molecular geometry (shape) of $\ce{SF4}$?
cards.body:
Seesaw.

$\ce{S}$ has 5 electron domains (4 bonds + 1 lone pair), so the electron geometry is **trigonal bipyramidal**. The lone pair sits in an equatorial position, which has fewer $90^\circ$ repulsions.

Example: $\ce{ClF3}$ (2 lone pairs) is T-shaped and $\ce{XeF2}$ (3 lone pairs) is linear.
cards.searchQuery: SF4 molecular geometry seesaw VSEPR

cards.title: What is the hybridization of the oxygen atom in $\ce{H2O}$?
cards.body:
$sp^3$

Count electron domains, not bonded atoms: 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 4 domains. The rule: 2 domains is $sp$, 3 is $sp^2$, 4 is $sp^3$.

Watch out: oxygen having only two bonds does not make it $sp$.
cards.searchQuery: hybridization of oxygen in water sp3 electron domains

cards.title: How many $\sigma$ bonds and how many $\pi$ bonds are in $\ce{HCN}$ ($\ce{H-C≡N}$)?
cards.body:
2 $\sigma$ bonds and 2 $\pi$ bonds.

Every single bond is one $\sigma$; a double bond is $\sigma + \pi$; a triple bond is $\sigma + 2\pi$. In $\ce{H-C≡N}$ that is one $\sigma$ for $\ce{C-H}$ plus $\sigma + 2\pi$ for the triple bond.

Why: $\sigma$ bonds form by head-on overlap, $\pi$ bonds by side-by-side overlap of unhybridized p orbitals, so $\pi$ bonds block rotation.
cards.searchQuery: sigma and pi bonds in HCN triple bond count

cards.title: Which of these molecules is polar: $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{BF3}$, $\ce{CCl4}$ or $\ce{SO2}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{SO2}$

The lone pair on $\ce{S}$ makes it bent, so the $\ce{S-O}$ bond dipoles don't cancel.

$\ce{CO2}$ (linear), $\ce{BF3}$ (trigonal planar) and $\ce{CCl4}$ (tetrahedral) all have polar bonds, but their **symmetric shapes** make the dipoles cancel.
Tip: polar molecule = polar bonds + an asymmetric shape.
cards.searchQuery: polar molecule SO2 bent dipoles cancel symmetric

cards.title: Rank by boiling point: propane ($\ce{CH3CH2CH3}$), dimethyl ether ($\ce{CH3OCH3}$), ethanol ($\ce{CH3CH2OH}$). All have molar masses near $45\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.
cards.body:
Propane ($-42\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) < dimethyl ether ($-24\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) < ethanol ($78\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

Similar size means similar dispersion forces, so the extra force decides: **dipole-dipole** for the ether, **hydrogen bonding** for ethanol.

Watch out: the ether has $\ce{O}$ but no $\ce{O-H}$, so it can't H-bond with itself. A donor needs $\ce{H}$ bonded directly to $\ce{N}$, $\ce{O}$ or $\ce{F}$.
cards.searchQuery: boiling point ranking propane dimethyl ether ethanol hydrogen bonding

cards.title: Which subatomic particle's count determines which element an atom is?
cards.body:
The proton: the number of protons is the atomic number, $Z$.

Changing the neutron count gives an isotope of the same element; changing the electron count gives an ion of the same element.

Example: every carbon atom has 6 protons.
cards.searchQuery: atomic number protons identify element

cards.title: Boron is 19.9% $^{10}\ce{B}$ ($10.013\,\mathrm{u}$) and 80.1% $^{11}\ce{B}$ ($11.009\,\mathrm{u}$). What is its average atomic mass, in u to 2 decimal places?
cards.body:
$10.81\,\mathrm{u}$

Take the abundance-weighted average, using fractions rather than percents: $(0.199)(10.013) + (0.801)(11.009) = 1.993 + 8.818$.

Tip: the average must lie closer to the mass of the more abundant isotope. Here 10.81 is near 11.009, as expected.
cards.searchQuery: average atomic mass boron isotopes weighted average

cards.title: Rank the isoelectronic ions $\ce{O^2-}$, $\ce{F^-}$, $\ce{Na^+}$ and $\ce{Mg^2+}$ from largest to smallest.
cards.body:
$\ce{O^2-} > \ce{F^-} > \ce{Na^+} > \ce{Mg^2+}$

All four have 10 electrons (the $\ce{Ne}$ configuration), so size depends only on nuclear charge: from 8 protons up to 12, the same electron cloud is pulled in tighter.

Example: radii in pm are about 140, 133, 102 and 72.
Key idea: among isoelectronic species, more protons means a smaller radius.
cards.searchQuery: isoelectronic ions radius order O2- F- Na+ Mg2+

cards.title: Is $\ce{Na^+}$ larger or smaller than a $\ce{Na}$ atom? Is $\ce{Cl^-}$ larger or smaller than a $\ce{Cl}$ atom?
cards.body:
$\ce{Na^+}$ is smaller than $\ce{Na}$; $\ce{Cl^-}$ is larger than $\ce{Cl}$.

$\ce{Na^+}$ has lost its entire 3s shell, and its remaining electrons feel the same 11 protons. $\ce{Cl^-}$ gains an electron in the same shell, so repulsion rises with no extra protons to hold it.

Key idea: **cations shrink, anions expand** relative to their parent atoms.
cards.searchQuery: cation smaller anion larger than parent atom ionic radius

cards.title: What is the energy of one photon of $500.\,\mathrm{nm}$ light? Give the number in units of $10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, to 3 significant figures.
cards.body:
$3.97\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$

$E = hc/\lambda = (6.626\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s})(2.998\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s})/(5.00\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m})$.

Watch out: convert nm to m first.
Example: for a mole of photons, multiply by $N_A$ to get about $239\,\mathrm{kJ}$.
cards.searchQuery: photon energy E = hc/lambda 500 nm

cards.title: Light below a metal's threshold frequency ejects no electrons. What happens if you make that light much brighter?
cards.body:
Still no electrons are ejected.

Each electron absorbs a **single photon**, and a photon's energy depends only on its frequency ($E = h\nu$), not on the light's intensity.

Above the threshold, brighter light ejects more electrons, but their maximum kinetic energy, $h\nu - \Phi$ ($\Phi$ is the work function), still depends only on frequency.
Key idea: intensity sets the number of photons; frequency sets the energy per photon.
cards.searchQuery: photoelectric effect threshold frequency intensity

cards.title: Bohr model: what is the energy of the hydrogen atom's electron in level $n$?
cards.body:
$E_n = -\dfrac{2.18\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{J}}{n^2}$, or $-13.6\,\mathrm{eV}/n^2$

Energy is lowest (most negative) at $n = 1$ and rises toward 0 as $n \to \infty$, where the electron is free.

Example: ionizing ground-state hydrogen takes $2.18\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{J}$ per atom, or $1312\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.
Watch out: the energies are negative; the zero of energy is the free electron.
cards.searchQuery: Bohr model hydrogen energy levels formula

cards.title: What wavelength of light does a hydrogen atom emit when its electron drops from $n = 3$ to $n = 2$? Answer in nm, to 3 significant figures.
cards.body:
$656\,\mathrm{nm}$ (red light).

$\Delta{E} = (2.18\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{J})(1/2^2 - 1/3^2) = 3.03\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, then $\lambda = hc/\Delta{E}$.

Key idea: all of hydrogen's visible lines end at $n = 2$ (the **Balmer series**).
cards.searchQuery: hydrogen n=3 to n=2 wavelength Balmer 656 nm

cards.title: Which hydrogen transition emits the highest-energy photon: $n = 2 \to 1$, $3 \to 2$, $4 \to 3$ or $5 \to 4$?
cards.body:
$n = 2 \to 1$

The levels crowd together as $n$ grows ($E_n \propto -1/n^2$), so the $2 \to 1$ gap, three-quarters of the ionization energy, dwarfs the gaps between higher levels.

Example: it is ultraviolet at $122\,\mathrm{nm}$, in the **Lyman series** (transitions ending at $n = 1$).
cards.searchQuery: hydrogen emission highest energy transition Lyman series

cards.title: What is the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ of a particle with mass $m$ and speed $v$?
cards.body:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$ (Planck's constant divided by momentum).

Every moving object has a wavelength, but only very light particles have one large enough to matter. Electron diffraction is the evidence.

Example: a thrown baseball's wavelength is around $10^{-34}\,\mathrm{m}$, far too small to detect.
cards.searchQuery: de Broglie wavelength h over mv

cards.title: What does each quantum number, $n$, $\ell$, $m_\ell$ and $m_s$, describe?
cards.body:
$n$: shell (size and energy). $\ell$: subshell shape. $m_\ell$: orbital orientation. $m_s$: electron spin.

- $\ell = 0, 1, 2, 3$ are s, p, d, f
- $m_\ell$ runs from $-\ell$ to $+\ell$
- $m_s = +\tfrac{1}{2}$ or $-\tfrac{1}{2}$

Key idea: the first three numbers specify an **orbital**; adding $m_s$ specifies one electron in it.
cards.searchQuery: four quantum numbers n l ml ms meaning

cards.title: Is this set of quantum numbers allowed: $n = 3$, $\ell = 1$, $m_\ell = -2$, $m_s = +\tfrac{1}{2}$?
cards.body:
No.

$m_\ell$ runs from $-\ell$ to $+\ell$, so $\ell = 1$ (a p subshell) allows only $-1$, $0$ and $+1$.

Tip: check $n \ge 1$; $0 \le \ell \le n - 1$; $|m_\ell| \le \ell$; $m_s = \pm\tfrac{1}{2}$.
cards.searchQuery: allowed quantum numbers rules ml range

cards.title: What is the maximum number of electrons in a subshell with $\ell = 2$?
cards.body:
10

$\ell = 2$ is a d subshell with $2\ell + 1 = 5$ orbitals ($m_\ell = -2$ to $+2$), each holding 2 electrons.

Tip: capacities are s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14.
cards.searchQuery: d subshell maximum electrons l=2

cards.title: How many radial nodes does a 3p orbital have?
cards.body:
1

Radial nodes $= n - \ell - 1 = 3 - 1 - 1 = 1$. Angular nodes $= \ell = 1$ (one nodal plane), so there are $n - 1 = 2$ nodes in total.

Example: a 3s orbital has 2 radial nodes and no angular nodes.
cards.searchQuery: radial nodes 3p orbital n minus l minus 1

cards.title: Which principle says no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers?
cards.body:
The Pauli exclusion principle.

No two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers. So an orbital (fixed $n$, $\ell$, $m_\ell$) holds at most 2 electrons, with opposite spins, $m_s = +\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $-\tfrac{1}{2}$.

Key idea: this is why subshell capacities are 2, 6, 10 and 14.
cards.searchQuery: Pauli exclusion principle four quantum numbers

cards.title: In the Aufbau filling order, which subshell fills immediately after 5s?
cards.body:
4d

Subshells fill in order of increasing $n + \ell$; for ties, lower $n$ first. So 5s ($5 + 0$) is followed by 4d ($4 + 2$), then 5p ($5 + 1$).

Example: the same rule puts 4s before 3d, and 4f after 6s.
cards.searchQuery: Aufbau filling order after 5s 4d

cards.title: Write the ground-state electron configuration of sulfur ($Z = 16$) in noble-gas shorthand.
cards.body:
$\mathrm{[Ne]\,3s^2\,3p^4}$

16 electrons: 10 in the neon core, then 2 in 3s and 4 in 3p.

Example: by Hund's rule, two of the four 3p electrons are unpaired, so a sulfur atom has **2 unpaired electrons**.
cards.searchQuery: sulfur electron configuration noble gas shorthand

cards.title: Iron is $\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^6\,4s^2}$. What is the ground-state electron configuration of $\ce{Fe^3+}$?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^5}$

Transition metals lose their **4s electrons first**, before any 3d electrons. $\ce{Fe^3+}$ loses both 4s electrons and one 3d.

Watch out: $\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^3\,4s^2}$ is the classic wrong answer.
Example: with five unpaired electrons, $\ce{Fe^3+}$ is strongly paramagnetic.
cards.searchQuery: Fe3+ electron configuration transition metal ion 4s first

cards.title: How many unpaired electrons does a gaseous $\ce{Fe^2+}$ ion have in its ground state?
cards.body:
4

$\ce{Fe^2+}$ is $\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^6}$. By Hund's rule, five electrons occupy the five 3d orbitals singly, and the sixth pairs with one of them.

Tip: write the d-orbital boxes and fill singly first; then count the lone arrows.
cards.searchQuery: Fe2+ unpaired electrons 3d6 Hund's rule

cards.title: Which of these ions is diamagnetic: $\ce{Zn^2+}$, $\ce{Fe^3+}$, $\ce{Cu^2+}$ or $\ce{Mn^2+}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{Zn^2+}$, which is $\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10}}$.

**Diamagnetic** means every electron is paired, so the substance is weakly repelled by a magnetic field. Any unpaired electron makes a species **paramagnetic** (attracted).

Example: $\ce{Fe^3+}$ and $\ce{Mn^2+}$ are $\mathrm{3d^5}$ (5 unpaired), and $\ce{Cu^2+}$ is $\mathrm{3d^9}$ (1 unpaired).
cards.searchQuery: diamagnetic ion Zn2+ paramagnetic unpaired electrons

cards.title: Estimate $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ for a valence electron of chlorine using $Z_\mathrm{eff} \approx Z - (\text{number of core electrons})$.
cards.body:
About $+7$ ($17 - 10$)

Core electrons shield almost completely, while same-shell electrons barely shield each other. Across period 3 this estimate climbs from $+1$ for $\ce{Na}$ to $+7$ for $\ce{Cl}$.

Why: that growing pull is why the atoms shrink and hold their electrons more tightly.
Example: Slater's rules give a more realistic $+6.1$ for chlorine.
cards.searchQuery: effective nuclear charge estimate chlorine Z minus core electrons

cards.title: Which atom is largest: $\ce{K}$, $\ce{Ca}$, $\ce{Br}$ or $\ce{Rb}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{Rb}$

It's the only one in period 5, so its valence electron occupies a higher shell. As a group 1 metal it also has the lowest $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ in its period.

Example: among the period-4 atoms, $\ce{K} > \ce{Ca} > \ce{Br}$.
Tip: compare period first (more shells wins), then group (further left wins).
cards.searchQuery: largest atomic radius K Ca Br Rb periodic trend

cards.title: Which has the lowest first ionization energy: $\ce{Na}$, $\ce{Mg}$, $\ce{Al}$ or $\ce{K}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{K}$ ($419\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, versus $496\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ for $\ce{Na}$)

Its 4s electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded than sodium's 3s electron.

Watch out: $\ce{Al}$ ($578\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$) is below $\ce{Mg}$ ($738\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$), because a 3p electron is easier to remove than a 3s electron.
cards.searchQuery: lowest first ionization energy potassium Na Mg Al

cards.title: Which releases more energy when a gaseous atom gains an electron: $\ce{F}$ or $\ce{Cl}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{Cl}$ ($349$ versus $328\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ released), even though $\ce{F}$ is more electronegative.

$\ce{F}$ is so small that an added electron is crowded by the seven valence electrons already there. That repulsion offsets its stronger nuclear attraction.

Key idea: chlorine has the most exothermic electron affinity of any element.
cards.searchQuery: electron affinity chlorine greater than fluorine

cards.title: Electron affinity is the energy change for which process? Write it for a generic element $\ce{X}$.
cards.body:
$\ce{X(g) + e^- -> X^-(g)}$

Electron affinity is defined for gaseous atoms. Most first electron affinities are negative (energy is released).

Watch out: adding a second electron, as in $\ce{O^-(g) + e^- -> O^2-(g)}$, always costs energy because the incoming electron is repelled by the anion.
cards.searchQuery: electron affinity definition gaseous atom gains electron equation

cards.title: In which directions does metallic character increase on the periodic table?
cards.body:
Down a group and to the left across a period (the opposite of the ionization energy trend).

Metallic character tracks how easily an atom gives up electrons. The most reactive metals ($\ce{Cs}$, $\ce{Fr}$) sit at the bottom left and the most reactive nonmetal ($\ce{F}$) at the top right.

Example: the **metalloids** lie along the staircase between them.
cards.searchQuery: metallic character periodic trend down group left

cards.title: What is the formula of aluminum oxide?
cards.body:
$\ce{Al2O3}$

The charges must cancel: two $\ce{Al^3+}$ give $+6$ and three $\ce{O^2-}$ give $-6$.

Tip: each ion's charge becomes the other's subscript, then reduce.
Watch out: $\ce{Mg^2+}$ and $\ce{O^2-}$ give $\ce{MgO}$, not $\ce{Mg2O2}$.
cards.searchQuery: aluminum oxide formula Al2O3 ionic charges

cards.title: What is the formula of iron(III) sulfate?
cards.body:
$\ce{Fe2(SO4)3}$

The Roman numeral gives iron's charge, $+3$, and sulfate is $\ce{SO4^2-}$. Two $\ce{Fe^3+}$ ($+6$) balance three $\ce{SO4^2-}$ ($-6$).

Watch out: keep parentheses around a polyatomic ion that takes a subscript.
cards.searchQuery: iron(III) sulfate formula Fe2(SO4)3

cards.title: What is the formula of the sulfite ion?
cards.body:
$\ce{SO3^2-}$

An **-ite** ion has one fewer oxygen than the **-ate** ion with the same charge: sulfate $\ce{SO4^2-}$ versus sulfite $\ce{SO3^2-}$, nitrate $\ce{NO3^-}$ versus nitrite $\ce{NO2^-}$.

Example: per-...-ate has one more O than -ate (perchlorate $\ce{ClO4^-}$); hypo-...-ite has one fewer than -ite (hypochlorite $\ce{ClO^-}$).
cards.searchQuery: sulfite ion formula SO3 2- polyatomic ate ite

cards.title: Born–Haber cycle for $\ce{NaCl}$, in kJ/mol: $\ce{Na}$ sublimation 107, $IE_1$ 496, half the $\ce{Cl-Cl}$ bond 122, $EA$ −349, $\Delta{H}_\mathrm{f}$ −411. Lattice energy, in kJ/mol?
cards.body:
$787\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, the energy needed to separate the solid into gaseous ions.

The direct path equals the sum of the steps: $-411 = 107 + 496 + 122 - 349 - U$, so $U = 787$.

Watch out: some textbooks define lattice energy for forming the lattice instead, which gives $-787\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.
cards.searchQuery: Born-Haber cycle NaCl lattice energy calculation

cards.title: Why doesn't solid $\ce{NaCl}$ conduct electricity, while molten or dissolved $\ce{NaCl}$ does?
cards.body:
In the solid, the ions are locked in place in the lattice; melting or dissolving frees them to move and carry charge.

Ionic solids have no mobile electrons, unlike metals.

Example: they're also **brittle**: shifting one layer of ions lines up like charges, which repel and split the crystal.
cards.searchQuery: why solid NaCl does not conduct electricity molten conducts

cards.title: How does the electron-sea model of metallic bonding explain why metals conduct electricity and are malleable?
cards.body:
Metal cations sit in a sea of delocalized valence electrons. The mobile electrons carry current, and because the bonding isn't directional, layers of cations can slide past each other.

Key idea: that sliding is why metals are **malleable** and ductile.
Example: ionic solids, by contrast, shatter when a shift pushes like charges together.
cards.searchQuery: electron sea model metallic bonding conductivity malleability

cards.title: Why does quartz ($\ce{SiO2}$) melt only above $1600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, while solid $\ce{CO2}$ sublimes at $-78\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
cards.body:
Quartz is a **covalent network solid**: melting it means breaking strong $\ce{Si-O}$ bonds throughout the crystal. Solid $\ce{CO2}$ is a **molecular solid**, held together only by weak dispersion forces between separate $\ce{O=C=O}$ molecules.

Why: silicon forms weak $\pi$ bonds, so instead of double bonds it makes four single bonds to $\ce{O}$, building a 3D network.
cards.searchQuery: quartz SiO2 network covalent solid vs CO2 molecular solid melting point

cards.title: How many valence electrons must the Lewis structure of the sulfate ion, $\ce{SO4^2-}$, show?
cards.body:
32

$\ce{S}$ contributes 6, the four $\ce{O}$ atoms contribute 24, and the $2-$ charge adds 2 more.

Tip: for a cation, subtract electrons instead: $\ce{NH4^+}$ has $5 + 4 - 1 = 8$.
cards.searchQuery: sulfate ion valence electrons Lewis structure count

cards.title: What are the three kinds of exceptions to the octet rule? Give an example of each.
cards.body:
Incomplete octet, odd number of electrons, expanded octet.

- Incomplete octet: $\ce{BF3}$ (boron has only 6 electrons)
- Odd electron count: $\ce{NO}$ and $\ce{NO2}$ (radicals)
- Expanded octet: $\ce{SF6}$ and $\ce{PCl5}$ (period 3 or below)

Why: an odd total electron count makes octets on every atom impossible.
cards.searchQuery: three exceptions to the octet rule examples

cards.title: Why can phosphorus form $\ce{PCl5}$, while nitrogen never forms $\ce{NCl5}$?
cards.body:
Nitrogen is a small period-2 atom with only four valence orbitals (2s and 2p), so it can't hold more than 8 electrons. Larger period-3 atoms like $\ce{P}$ can accommodate more than four electron pairs.

Why: intro textbooks credit phosphorus's empty 3d orbitals; modern bonding models attribute it mainly to size.
Key idea: no expanded octets in period 2.
cards.searchQuery: why phosphorus PCl5 but nitrogen no NCl5 expanded octet

cards.title: In one resonance structure of nitrate, $\ce{NO3^-}$ (one $\ce{N=O}$ and two $\ce{N-O}$ bonds), what is the formal charge on nitrogen?
cards.body:
$+1$

$FC = V - N - B/2 = 5 - 0 - 8/2 = +1$.

Check: each single-bonded $\ce{O}$ is $-1$ ($6 - 6 - 1$) and the double-bonded $\ce{O}$ is 0, so the formal charges sum to the ion's charge, $-1$.
cards.searchQuery: formal charge nitrogen nitrate ion resonance structure

cards.title: Using formal charges, how do you pick the best of several valid Lewis structures?
cards.body:
Choose the structure whose formal charges are closest to zero. If a negative formal charge is needed, put it on the most electronegative atom.

Example: for $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{O=C=O}$ (all zeros) beats a structure with $+1$ and $-1$ charges.

Tip: the formal charges must always sum to the species' overall charge.
cards.searchQuery: choose best Lewis structure formal charge rules

cards.title: True or false: a molecule with several resonance structures rapidly flips back and forth between them.
cards.body:
False.

The molecule has one real structure, the **resonance hybrid**, a weighted average of the drawn structures. A single Lewis structure just can't show delocalized electrons.

Example: ozone has two identical $\ce{O-O}$ bonds (bond order 1.5) at all times.
cards.searchQuery: resonance structures misconception hybrid ozone bond order

cards.title: What is the average carbon–oxygen bond order in the carbonate ion, $\ce{CO3^2-}$?
cards.body:
$\tfrac{4}{3} \approx 1.33$

Three equivalent resonance structures share one $\ce{C=O}$ double bond among three positions: 4 bonds spread over 3 $\ce{C-O}$ links.

Key idea: all three bonds are the same length, between a single and a double bond.
cards.searchQuery: carbonate ion carbon oxygen bond order resonance

cards.title: How many neutrons are in an atom of $^{14}\ce{C}$? (Carbon has $Z = 6$.)
cards.body:
8

Neutrons $= A - Z = 14 - 6$. The mass number $A$ counts **protons plus neutrons**.

Example: $^{12}\ce{C}$ has 6 neutrons; $^{14}\ce{C}$ is the radioactive isotope used in radiocarbon dating.
Watch out: the mass number is not the neutron count.
cards.searchQuery: neutrons in carbon-14 mass number minus atomic number

cards.title: How many electrons does an $\ce{Mg^2+}$ ion have? ($Z = 12$)
cards.body:
10

A neutral $\ce{Mg}$ atom has 12 electrons; the $2+$ charge means it has **lost 2**. The ion is isoelectronic with $\ce{Ne}$.

Tip: a positive charge means fewer electrons than protons, a negative charge means more.
cards.searchQuery: electrons in magnesium 2+ ion charge

cards.title: What did Rutherford's gold-foil experiment show about the structure of the atom?
cards.body:
Nearly all of an atom's mass and positive charge sit in a tiny, dense **nucleus**; the rest of the atom is mostly empty space.

Most $\alpha$ particles passed straight through the foil, a few were deflected at large angles, and a very few bounced almost straight back.

Watch out: Thomson's "plum pudding" model predicted only small deflections, which is why the results were a surprise.
cards.searchQuery: Rutherford gold foil experiment conclusion nucleus

cards.title: How is the atomic mass unit ($\mathrm{u}$) defined?
cards.body:
$\tfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of one $^{12}\ce{C}$ atom.

Numerically, $1\,\mathrm{u} \approx 1.6605\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$. A proton or neutron is close to $1\,\mathrm{u}$.

Key idea: this is why the molar mass of an element in g/mol matches its atomic mass in u.
cards.searchQuery: atomic mass unit definition one twelfth carbon-12

cards.title: How many valence electrons does an atom in group 16, such as $\ce{S}$, have?
cards.body:
6

For main-group elements, the **group number's last digit** gives the valence electron count: group 1 has 1, group 14 has 4, group 18 has 8 (2 for $\ce{He}$).

Example: oxygen, sulfur and selenium all have the configuration $ns^2np^4$ in their valence shell.
cards.searchQuery: valence electrons group 16 chalcogens number

cards.title: Write the ground-state electron configuration of phosphorus ($Z = 15$) in noble-gas shorthand.
cards.body:
$\mathrm{[Ne]\,3s^2\,3p^3}$

15 electrons: 10 in the neon core, then 2 in 3s and 3 in 3p. By Hund's rule, the three 3p electrons are unpaired.

Tip: the period number tells you the valence shell ($n = 3$), and the group tells you how many electrons are in it (5).
cards.searchQuery: phosphorus electron configuration noble gas shorthand

cards.title: What is the ground-state electron configuration of $\ce{Cu^+}$? (Copper atom: $\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10}\,4s^1}$.)
cards.body:
$\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10}}$

The 4s electron is removed first, leaving a **completely filled 3d subshell**. All electrons are paired, so $\ce{Cu^+}$ is diamagnetic.

Example: $\ce{Cu^2+}$ removes one 3d electron too and is $\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^9}$, which has one unpaired electron.
cards.searchQuery: Cu+ copper(I) ion electron configuration 3d10

cards.title: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state manganese atom ($Z = 25$) have?
cards.body:
5

Manganese is $\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^5\,4s^2}$. The five 3d electrons occupy five separate orbitals with parallel spins (Hund's rule), and the 4s electrons are paired.

Key idea: a half-filled d subshell gives the **maximum number of unpaired electrons** for the d block.
cards.searchQuery: manganese unpaired electrons 3d5 Hund

cards.title: Is a ground-state zinc atom ($\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10}\,4s^2}$) paramagnetic or diamagnetic? (Type one word.)
cards.body:
Diamagnetic.

Both the filled 3d subshell and the filled 4s orbital contain only paired electrons, so there is **no net magnetic moment** and the atom is weakly repelled by a magnetic field.

Example: $\ce{He}$, $\ce{Mg}$ and $\ce{Ca}$ atoms are diamagnetic for the same reason; $\ce{Na}$ (one unpaired 3s electron) is paramagnetic.
cards.searchQuery: zinc atom diamagnetic or paramagnetic paired electrons

cards.title: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the $n = 4$ shell?
cards.body:
32

The shell holds $2n^2 = 2(16) = 32$ electrons: 4s (2), 4p (6), 4d (10) and 4f (14).

Tip: the first four shell capacities are 2, 8, 18 and 32.
cards.searchQuery: maximum electrons n=4 shell 2n squared

cards.title: Which has the smallest radius: $\ce{S^2-}$, $\ce{Cl^-}$, $\ce{K^+}$ or $\ce{Ca^2+}$? (Type the ion, e.g. Na+.)
cards.body:
$\ce{Ca^2+}$

All four have 18 electrons (the $\ce{Ar}$ configuration), so the species with the **most protons** pulls the cloud in tightest. $\ce{Ca^2+}$ has 20 protons; $\ce{S^2-}$ has only 16.

Key idea: for isoelectronic species, radius decreases as nuclear charge increases.
cards.searchQuery: smallest isoelectronic ion Ca2+ K+ Cl- S2- radius

cards.title: Which has the largest second ionization energy: $\ce{Na}$, $\ce{Mg}$ or $\ce{Al}$? (Type the symbol.)
cards.body:
$\ce{Na}$

Removing a second electron from $\ce{Na^+}$ means breaking into the **noble-gas core** ($\mathrm{2p^6}$), which costs about $4560\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. For $\ce{Mg}$ ($1451$) and $\ce{Al}$ ($1817$) the second electron is still a valence electron.

Tip: the element just after a noble gas has the largest $IE_2$ in its period.
cards.searchQuery: largest second ionization energy sodium noble gas core

cards.title: Why does atomic radius change only slightly across the 3d transition metals, from $\ce{Sc}$ to $\ce{Zn}$?
cards.body:
The added electrons go into the inner 3d subshell, where they **shield** the outer 4s electrons from the growing nuclear charge.

So $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ on the 4s electrons rises only slightly, and the radius barely shrinks. Across main-group elements the added electrons go in the outer shell instead, which shields poorly.
cards.searchQuery: transition metals atomic radius nearly constant d electrons shielding

cards.title: What is the lanthanide contraction, and what is one consequence?
cards.body:
The steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanides (La to Lu) because 4f electrons **shield poorly** as nuclear charge grows.

Consequence: the period-6 transition metals have nearly the same radii as the period-5 metals above them, so $\ce{Zr}$ and $\ce{Hf}$ behave very similarly and are hard to separate.
cards.searchQuery: lanthanide contraction 4f shielding Zr Hf radius

cards.title: In which group of the periodic table are the halogens? (Number only.)
cards.body:
Group 17

The halogens are $\ce{F}$, $\ce{Cl}$, $\ce{Br}$, $\ce{I}$ and $\ce{At}$. Each has 7 valence electrons ($ns^2np^5$) and readily gains one electron to form $X^-$.

Example: the alkali metals are group 1, the alkaline earth metals group 2, and the noble gases group 18.
cards.searchQuery: halogens group number periodic table group 17

cards.title: Light has a wavelength of $600.\,\mathrm{nm}$. What is its frequency, in units of $10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$? (Number only, 3 significant figures; use $c = 3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.)
cards.body:
$5.00\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$

$c = \lambda\nu$, so $\nu = \dfrac{3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}}{6.00\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}}$.

Watch out: convert nm to m ($1\,\mathrm{nm} = 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}$) before dividing.
cards.searchQuery: frequency from wavelength c = lambda nu 600 nm

cards.title: Rank by increasing photon energy: visible light, X-rays, microwaves, ultraviolet.
cards.body:
Microwaves < visible < ultraviolet < X-rays.

Photon energy $E = h\nu = hc/\lambda$, so higher frequency and shorter wavelength mean **more energy per photon**.

Mnemonic: the full order is radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
cards.searchQuery: electromagnetic spectrum order photon energy microwave visible UV X-ray

cards.title: A photon with energy $4.0\,\mathrm{eV}$ strikes a metal with work function $\Phi = 2.5\,\mathrm{eV}$. What is the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron, in eV? (Number only.)
cards.body:
$1.5\,\mathrm{eV}$

$KE_\mathrm{max} = h\nu - \Phi = 4.0 - 2.5$. The work function is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the metal.

Watch out: if $h\nu < \Phi$, no electrons are ejected, no matter how intense the light.
cards.searchQuery: photoelectric effect maximum kinetic energy work function

cards.title: State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle for position and momentum.
cards.body:
$\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$

The more precisely a particle's position is known, the less precisely its momentum can be known, and vice versa.

Why: this is a property of matter waves, not a limit of our instruments. It is why electrons can't follow Bohr's fixed orbits and are described by orbitals instead.
cards.searchQuery: Heisenberg uncertainty principle position momentum h over 4 pi

cards.title: How much energy must a ground-state hydrogen atom absorb to reach $n = 2$, in eV? (Number only, 3 significant figures.)
cards.body:
$10.2\,\mathrm{eV}$

$\Delta E = 13.6\,\mathrm{eV}\left(\dfrac{1}{1^2} - \dfrac{1}{2^2}\right) = 13.6 \times \dfrac{3}{4}$.

Key idea: an atom absorbs only photons whose energy **exactly matches** the gap between levels.
cards.searchQuery: hydrogen n=1 to n=2 excitation energy eV Bohr

cards.title: How much energy, in kJ/mol, is needed to remove the electron from hydrogen atoms in the $n = 2$ level? (Number only, 3 significant figures; ionization from $n = 1$ takes $1312\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.)
cards.body:
$328\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$

Energy scales as $1/n^2$: $\dfrac{1312}{2^2} = 328$.

Watch out: the electron in $n = 2$ is already partway out, so ionizing it takes only a quarter of the ground-state energy.
cards.searchQuery: ionization energy hydrogen n=2 kJ/mol Bohr 1/n^2

cards.title: How many nodes (radial plus angular) does a 4f orbital have? (Number only.)
cards.body:
3

Total nodes $= n - 1 = 3$. A 4f orbital has $\ell = 3$ angular nodes and $n - \ell - 1 = 0$ radial nodes.

Tip: radial nodes $= n - \ell - 1$; angular nodes $= \ell$; they add up to $n - 1$.
cards.searchQuery: total nodes 4f orbital n minus 1 radial angular

cards.title: What is the formula of calcium phosphate? (Type it as plain text, e.g. Mg(OH)2.)
cards.body:
$\ce{Ca3(PO4)2}$

Calcium is $\ce{Ca^2+}$ and phosphate is $\ce{PO4^3-}$. The least common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6, so 3 calcium ($+6$) balance 2 phosphate ($-6$).

Watch out: put parentheses around the polyatomic ion when it takes a subscript.
cards.searchQuery: calcium phosphate formula Ca3(PO4)2 ionic charges

cards.title: What is the formula of ammonium sulfate? (Type it as plain text.)
cards.body:
$\ce{(NH4)2SO4}$

Ammonium is $\ce{NH4^+}$ and sulfate is $\ce{SO4^2-}$, so two ammonium ions balance one sulfate.

Tip: the only common polyatomic cation is $\ce{NH4^+}$; most other polyatomic ions are anions.
cards.searchQuery: ammonium sulfate formula (NH4)2SO4

cards.title: What is the systematic name of $\ce{Cu2O}$? (Type it with the Roman numeral, e.g. iron(III) oxide.)
cards.body:
Copper(I) oxide

Oxide is $\ce{O^2-}$, so two copper ions must carry $+2$ in total: each is $\ce{Cu+}$.

Watch out: transition metals with several common charges need a **Roman numeral**. $\ce{CuO}$ is copper(II) oxide.
cards.searchQuery: name of Cu2O copper(I) oxide Roman numeral

cards.title: Compare a $\ce{C-C}$ single bond, a $\ce{C=C}$ double bond and a $\ce{C#C}$ triple bond in length and strength.
cards.body:
Length: single > double > triple. Strength: triple > double > single.

Typical values: about 154, 134 and 120 pm, and about 347, 614 and 839 kJ/mol.

Why: more shared electron pairs pull the nuclei closer together and take more energy to break.
Watch out: the triple bond is not three times as strong as a single bond, because the $\pi$ bonds are weaker than the $\sigma$ bond.
cards.searchQuery: bond length bond strength single double triple carbon bonds

cards.title: Which bond is the most polar: $\ce{C-H}$, $\ce{C-N}$, $\ce{C-O}$ or $\ce{C-F}$? (Type the bond, e.g. C-H.)
cards.body:
$\ce{C-F}$

Polarity grows with the **electronegativity difference**. Using Pauling values, $\ce{C}$ is 2.55 and $\ce{F}$ is 3.98, a difference of 1.43, versus 0.89 for $\ce{C-O}$, 0.49 for $\ce{C-N}$ and 0.35 for $\ce{C-H}$.

Example: in a polar bond the more electronegative atom carries the partial negative charge, $\delta^-$.
cards.searchQuery: most polar bond electronegativity difference C-F C-O C-N C-H

cards.title: How many valence electrons must the Lewis structure of the nitrate ion, $\ce{NO3^-}$, show? (Number only.)
cards.body:
24

$\ce{N}$ contributes 5, three $\ce{O}$ atoms contribute 18, and the $1-$ charge adds 1.

Tip: add one electron per unit of negative charge; subtract one per unit of positive charge.
cards.searchQuery: nitrate ion valence electrons total Lewis structure

cards.title: How many lone pairs are on the central atom of $\ce{XeF4}$? (Number only.)
cards.body:
2

$\ce{Xe}$ has 8 valence electrons; four are shared in the four $\ce{Xe-F}$ bonds, leaving 4 electrons, which is **2 lone pairs**.

Key idea: 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs gives 6 electron domains, an octahedral arrangement with the lone pairs on opposite sides.
cards.searchQuery: XeF4 lone pairs on xenon central atom

cards.title: What is the bond order of $\ce{N2}$ according to molecular orbital theory? (Number only.)
cards.body:
3

Bond order $= \dfrac{(\text{bonding electrons}) - (\text{antibonding electrons})}{2}$. $\ce{N2}$ has 10 valence electrons: 8 bonding and 2 antibonding, so $(8 - 2)/2 = 3$.

Example: $\ce{He2}$ would have bond order 0 (2 bonding, 2 antibonding), which is why helium is monatomic.
cards.searchQuery: N2 bond order molecular orbital theory formula

cards.title: Why is $\ce{O2}$ paramagnetic, even though its Lewis structure shows no unpaired electrons?
cards.body:
Molecular orbital theory puts the last two valence electrons in two **degenerate $\pi^*$ orbitals**, one each with parallel spins (Hund's rule), so $\ce{O2}$ has 2 unpaired electrons.

Evidence: liquid oxygen is attracted to a magnet.
Key idea: the Lewis model gets bond order 2 right but cannot predict this magnetism.
cards.searchQuery: O2 paramagnetic molecular orbital theory pi star unpaired electrons

cards.title: What is the molecular geometry of $\ce{NH3}$, and roughly what is the $\ce{H-N-H}$ bond angle?
cards.body:
Trigonal pyramidal, about $107^\circ$.

$\ce{N}$ has 4 electron domains (3 bonds + 1 lone pair), so the electron geometry is tetrahedral. The lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly, squeezing the angle below $109.5^\circ$.

Tip: lone pairs take up more space than bonding pairs, so the ranking is LP-LP > LP-BP > BP-BP.
cards.searchQuery: NH3 molecular geometry trigonal pyramidal bond angle lone pair

cards.title: What is the $\ce{H-O-H}$ bond angle in water, in degrees? (Number only, 1 decimal place.)
cards.body:
$104.5^\circ$

$\ce{O}$ has 4 electron domains (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs), a tetrahedral electron geometry with a **bent** molecular shape. The two lone pairs compress the angle further below $109.5^\circ$ than the single lone pair does in $\ce{NH3}$ ($107^\circ$).
cards.searchQuery: water bond angle 104.5 bent VSEPR

cards.title: What is the molecular geometry of $\ce{XeF4}$? (Type the shape.)
cards.body:
Square planar.

Six electron domains give an octahedral electron geometry. The two lone pairs occupy **opposite** positions to minimize repulsion, leaving the four $\ce{F}$ atoms in a plane with $90^\circ$ angles.

Example: $\ce{ICl4^-}$ is also square planar.
cards.searchQuery: XeF4 molecular geometry square planar VSEPR

cards.title: What is the molecular geometry of the triiodide ion, $\ce{I3^-}$? (Type the shape.)
cards.body:
Linear.

The central $\ce{I}$ has 2 bonds and 3 lone pairs, so 5 domains in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement. The three lone pairs sit in the **equatorial plane**, leaving the two bonded atoms on the axis at $180^\circ$.

Example: $\ce{XeF2}$ is linear for the same reason.
cards.searchQuery: triiodide ion I3- molecular geometry linear three lone pairs

cards.title: What is the ideal $\ce{H-C-H}$ bond angle in methane, in degrees? (Number only, 1 decimal place.)
cards.body:
$109.5^\circ$

Four equivalent bonding domains point to the corners of a **tetrahedron**, which maximizes the separation between them.

Why: the angle is $\arccos(-1/3) \approx 109.47^\circ$.
cards.searchQuery: methane tetrahedral bond angle 109.5 degrees

cards.title: What is the hybridization of sulfur in $\ce{SF6}$? (Type it as plain text, e.g. sp3.)
cards.body:
$sp^3d^2$

Six bonding domains require six hybrid orbitals, giving an **octahedral** arrangement with $90^\circ$ angles.

Why: one s, three p and two d orbitals mix. (Many modern treatments favor bonding models without d orbitals, but exam answers use this count.)
cards.searchQuery: SF6 sulfur hybridization sp3d2 octahedral

cards.title: What is the hybridization of the carbon atom in $\ce{CO2}$? (Type it as plain text.)
cards.body:
$sp$

Carbon has 2 electron domains (two double bonds), so it uses two $sp$ hybrid orbitals for the $\sigma$ bonds. The two unhybridized p orbitals form the two $\pi$ bonds.

Key idea: 2 domains is $sp$ (linear, $180^\circ$).
cards.searchQuery: CO2 carbon hybridization sp linear pi bonds

cards.title: How many $\sigma$ bonds and how many $\pi$ bonds are in ethyne, $\ce{HC#CH}$?
cards.body:
3 $\sigma$ and 2 $\pi$.

The $\ce{C#C}$ triple bond is one $\sigma$ plus two $\pi$, and each $\ce{C-H}$ bond is one $\sigma$.

Why: each carbon is $sp$ hybridized; its two unhybridized p orbitals overlap sideways to make the two $\pi$ bonds.
cards.searchQuery: ethyne acetylene sigma pi bonds count hybridization

cards.title: What is the hybridization of each carbon in benzene, and what forms its delocalized $\pi$ system?
cards.body:
Each carbon is $sp^2$. The six unhybridized p orbitals overlap side by side above and below the ring, delocalizing six $\pi$ electrons.

This delocalization is why all six $\ce{C-C}$ bonds are equal in length (between single and double) and why benzene is unusually stable.
cards.searchQuery: benzene sp2 carbons delocalized pi system six electrons

cards.title: Which has the highest boiling point: $\ce{HF}$, $\ce{HCl}$, $\ce{HBr}$ or $\ce{HI}$? (Type the formula.)
cards.body:
$\ce{HF}$

Hydrogen bonding in $\ce{HF}$ gives it a boiling point of about $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, versus $-85$, $-67$ and $-35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for $\ce{HCl}$, $\ce{HBr}$ and $\ce{HI}$.

Watch out: among the other three, boiling point rises with size ($\ce{HCl} < \ce{HBr} < \ce{HI}$) because dispersion forces grow.
cards.searchQuery: hydrogen halide boiling points HF hydrogen bonding

cards.title: Pentane boils at $36\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and its isomer neopentane at $9.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Why is neopentane's boiling point lower?
cards.body:
Neopentane is compact and nearly spherical, so it has **less surface contact** between molecules and weaker dispersion forces. Pentane is long and chain-like and packs better.

Both have the same formula, $\ce{C5H12}$, and the same molar mass, so shape is the only difference.
Key idea: for similar molecules, more branching means a lower boiling point.
cards.searchQuery: pentane neopentane boiling point branching dispersion forces surface area

cards.title: Which intermolecular force is mainly responsible for dissolving $\ce{NaCl}$ in water? (Type the force.)
cards.body:
Ion-dipole forces.

Water's partial negative end ($\ce{O}$) surrounds $\ce{Na^+}$ and its partial positive ends ($\ce{H}$) surround $\ce{Cl^-}$. The energy released by these attractions (hydration) compensates for breaking the lattice.

Tip: ion-dipole is the strongest of the intermolecular forces.
cards.searchQuery: ion-dipole force dissolving NaCl in water hydration

cards.title: Why does graphite conduct electricity while diamond does not?
cards.body:
In graphite each carbon is $sp^2$ and has one leftover p electron that is **delocalized** across its layer, so electrons can move. In diamond every carbon is $sp^3$ and all four valence electrons are locked in $\sigma$ bonds.

Graphite is also soft because its layers are held together only by weak dispersion forces and slide past one another.
cards.searchQuery: graphite conducts electricity diamond does not sp2 delocalized electrons
